chunks.subtopicName: Demand for and supply of labour
chunks.heading: What is a labour market?
chunks.body: A labour market is where people who want jobs meet employers who want workers. Workers offer their labour, and employers offer wages in return.
chunks.checkText: In a labour market, who is offering labour?

chunks.subtopicName: Demand for and supply of labour
chunks.heading: Why firms want workers
chunks.body: Firms don't want labour for its own sake. They demand workers only because they need them to make the goods and services that customers want.

chunks.heading: Cheaper labour, more workers hired

chunks.heading: A booming economy needs more workers

chunks.heading: Some industries grow, others shrink

chunks.heading: The skills a worker brings

chunks.heading: Who counts as part of the workforce?

chunks.heading: A bigger population, a bigger workforce

chunks.heading: An older population, a smaller workforce

chunks.subtopicName: Demand for and supply of labour
chunks.heading: Where wages settle
chunks.body: Labour market equilibrium happens where the [[econ-labour-supply-curve|supply]] of workers matches the [[econ-labour-demand-curve|demand]] from firms. At this wage, everyone willing to work finds a job.

checkOptions.text: Quantity of labour supplied equals quantity demanded
Wages are at their highest possible level
All workers earn exactly the same wage

chunks.body: Just like other markets produce a price and a quantity, the labour market produces two outcomes: wage levels and how many people are employed.

chunks.body: Average weekly earnings is the typical amount all employees are paid before tax each week. It's a simple way to track wage trends over time.
